questiontext.text: What problem is a Bloom filter primarily designed to solve?

answer.text: Space-efficient probabilistic set-membership testing

feedback.text: Correct — it answers "is x possibly in the set?" using very little memory.

answer.text: Keeping elements in sorted order for range queries

feedback.text: No — a Bloom filter stores no order and cannot enumerate elements.

answer.text: Estimating the frequency of items in a stream

feedback.text: That is a Count-Min Sketch; a Bloom filter only tracks membership.

answer.text: Exact retrieval of stored key-value pairs

feedback.text: No — it stores no keys or values, only bits.

generalfeedback.text: A Bloom filter is a compact probabilistic structure for set-membership queries; it trades a small false-positive rate for large space savings.

questiontext.text: What are the two core components of a standard Bloom filter?

answer.text: A bit array of size m and k independent hash functions

feedback.text: Correct — insert sets k bits, query checks the same k bits.

answer.text: A balanced binary search tree and a comparator

feedback.text: No — Bloom filters use no tree and no comparisons.

answer.text: A 2D counter array and d hash functions

feedback.text: That describes a Count-Min Sketch, not a Bloom filter.

answer.text: A linked list of buckets with random heights

feedback.text: That describes a skip list, not a Bloom filter.

generalfeedback.text: A Bloom filter is a bit array of m bits plus k hash functions; inserting an item sets the k hashed positions to 1.

questiontext.text: A Bloom filter query returns "possibly present" for an item. What can you conclude?

answer.text: The item may be present or may be a false positive; you cannot be certain

feedback.text: Correct — a "possibly present" answer can be a false positive.

answer.text: The item is definitely in the set

feedback.text: No — collisions can set all k bits without the item ever being inserted.

answer.text: The item was inserted exactly once

feedback.text: No — a Bloom filter cannot count insertions.

answer.text: The item is definitely absent

feedback.text: No — "definitely absent" corresponds to at least one bit being 0.

generalfeedback.text: If any of the k bits is 0 the item is definitely absent; if all are 1 the item is only possibly present (false positives are allowed).

questiontext.text: The false-positive rate of a Bloom filter depends on which quantities?

answer.text: The bit-array size m, the number of inserted items n, and the number of hashes k

feedback.text: Correct — more bits per item lowers the rate; k can be tuned to minimize it.

answer.text: Only the values of the items inserted

feedback.text: No — the rate is governed by m, n, and k, not the specific values.

answer.text: The recursion depth of the queries

feedback.text: No — queries are not recursive and take fixed O(k) time.

answer.text: Whether the array is kept sorted

feedback.text: No — a Bloom filter has no notion of order.

generalfeedback.text: With m bits, n items, and k hashes the false-positive probability is approximately (1 - e^(-kn/m))^k, minimized when k = (m/n) ln 2.

questiontext.text: A standard Bloom filter never produces a false negative: if an item was inserted, a query for it always returns "possibly present".

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — inserting sets the k bits to 1, so a later query for that item always finds them set.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: No — bits are only ever set to 1, never cleared, so inserted items are never reported absent.

questiontext.text: A standard (non-counting) Bloom filter supports deleting an item by clearing its k bits to 0.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — clearing a bit could break another item that shares it, introducing false negatives.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — a standard Bloom filter cannot delete; shared bits make clearing unsafe (counting Bloom filters are needed for deletion).

questiontext.text: A Bloom filter may wrongly report an absent item as present. This kind of error is called a ______ (two words).

answer.text: false positive

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: false positive*

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: positive

feedback.text: Correct — the error is a false positive.

questiontext.text: Which statements about a standard Bloom filter are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It is very compact because it stores no actual keys

feedback.text: Yes — only a bit array is kept, giving large space savings.

answer.text: It can have false positives but never false negatives

feedback.text: Yes — the asymmetric error is its defining property.

answer.text: It can list all the elements currently stored

feedback.text: No — it stores no keys, so enumeration is impossible.

answer.text: It supports arbitrary deletion out of the box

feedback.text: No — a standard Bloom filter cannot delete items.

generalfeedback.text: A Bloom filter is compact and stores no keys; it allows false positives but no false negatives, cannot enumerate, and cannot delete.
